pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — explain the pattern in zeros when multiplying by powers of 10 and in decimal-point placement when ×/÷ by a power of 10; use whole-number exponents for powers of 10 (10³ = 1000).
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5/Y6 multiply and divide whole numbers and decimals by 10, 100 and 1000; exponent notation is a US-forward extension of the same ×10 structure.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.A.2 — 'Explain patterns in the number of zeros of the product when multiplying a number by powers of 10, and explain patterns in the placement of the decimal point when a decimal is multiplied or divided by a power of 10. Use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10.'
• Operational details: Build exponent as a COUNT of factors of 10 (10³ = 10×10×10), then connect the exponent to both the zero-count in whole-number products AND the number of places the digits shift. Emphasise that DIGITS shift, the point stays; the exponent tells you how many places. Predict-then-check with a place-value chart before generalising.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'Write 10⁴ as an ordinary number and say how many zeros.' Tier B: 'Explain why 3.4 × 10² = 340 using the digit shift.' Tier C: 'Predict 2.56 × 10³ without calculating and justify the pattern.'
bestPractices: Define an exponent as the number of factors of 10 (10³ = 10×10×10), never as 'the number of zeros' — the zero-count is a CONSEQUENCE for whole numbers that breaks for decimals
Tie the exponent simultaneously to zeros in a whole-number product and to the number of places the digits shift, so the child sees them as the same pattern
Insist that the digits move and the decimal point stays fixed — explicitly reject 'move the decimal point'
Use predict-then-check on a place-value chart before stating the generalisation
Include ÷ by powers of 10 alongside × so the pattern is bidirectional and exponents are seen to shift digits the other way
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart with digits sliding N columns for ×10^N (point fixed)
Expanded factor strings: 10³ = 10×10×10 = 1000 with zeros tallied
Exponent stepper linking 10¹, 10², 10³ to 10, 100, 1000 and their zero counts
Arrow cards showing 3.4 → 34 → 340 with '×10' per hop
commonMisconceptions: 'Multiplying by a power of 10 just adds zeros' — fails for decimals (3.4 × 100 ≠ 3.400)
Reading 10³ as 10×3 = 30 (confusing exponent with a factor)
Believing the decimal point moves rather than the digits
Miscounting the shift — shifting by the base (10) rather than the exponent (3)
Assuming the exponent equals the number of digits in the result rather than factors of ten

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: explain the patterns in zeros when multiplying whole numbers by powers of ten, and the decimal-point placement when multiplying or dividing decimals by a power of ten, using whole-number exponents (10³ = 1000). The central idea is that an exponent counts factors of ten (10³ = 10×10×10) and equals the number of place-value columns the digits shift; the digits move while the decimal point stays fixed. The 'add zeros' shortcut is a consequence for whole numbers only and breaks for decimals (3.4 × 100 = 340, not 3.400); any zeros that do appear are placeholders for emptied whole-number columns, not zeros glued onto the original digits.

activities.title: Sweep the exponent on a place-value chart
feedback: If a learner writes 3.400 for 3.4 × 100, show on the chart that each ×10 slides the digits one column left: 3.4 → 34 → 340. The answer is 340, not 3.400 — the digits moved into larger columns and a single zero fills the now-empty ones place, rather than zeros being appended after the decimal point.

If the digits move the wrong way, anchor direction: multiplying a positive number by 10, 100 or 1000 makes it bigger, so digits travel to larger (left-hand) columns; dividing by these makes it smaller, so they move right.
If a learner shifts by 10 instead of by 3 for 10³, re-read the exponent: the little 3 is how many columns, not the base.

Confirm success when the learner predicts the number of columns from the exponent before moving any digit and explains that any zero appearing in the product is a placeholder for an emptied column, not a zero appended to the original digits.
activities.rationale: A live, predict-then-check representation lets the learner see the exponent, the zero-count and the shift-distance change together, which is what can turn a rule into a visible pattern. Including division makes the pattern bidirectional.
sourceClaims: Y5/Y6 pupils multiply and divide whole numbers and decimals by 10, 100 and 1000.
5.NBT.A.2: explain patterns in zeros and decimal-point placement for ×/÷ by powers of 10 and use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10.
learnerActions: Place a number — e.g. 3.4 — on a place-value chart with the decimal point marked in a fixed position.

Set a power of ten (10¹, then 10², then 10³) and, for each, slide every digit left by the number shown in the exponent; the column count is the total shift from 3.4 and equals the exponent: 3.4 → 34 (10¹, one column) → 340 (10², two columns) → 3400 (10³, three columns), keeping the point pinned.
Alongside, write the power in expanded form (10³ = 10×10×10 = 1000) and tally its zeros.
State in words: 'The exponent tells me how many columns the digits jump.'
Repeat with division by powers of ten (shifting digits the other way, e.g. 3.4 ÷ 10 = 0.34) and with a whole number like 7 (7 × 10 = 70) to compare where zeros appear.
activities.intendedInsight: The exponent equals the number of place-value columns the digits shift, so 'powers of ten' and 'place-value shift' are the same idea. For a decimal like 3.4, multiplying by 10 does not append a zero (3.4 × 10 = 34, not 3.40); any zeros appearing in larger products such as 340 or 3400 are placeholders filling emptied whole-number columns, not zeros glued onto the original number — so the 'add-a-zero' rule is not the real pattern.

activities.title: Reference ladder of powers of ten
feedback: If a learner reads 10³ as 30, unpack it as repeated multiplication 10×10×10 = 1000 and set it beside 10×3 = 30.

If a learner says the exponent is 'the number of zeros' as a definition, restate it as the number of factors of ten — the zero-count of the power is a result, and using it as an 'add that many zeros' rule fails for decimals (3.4 × 100 = 340, not 3.400).
This ladder is a static reference; pair it with the moving chart so the digit shift is seen as an action, not only read.
activities.rationale: A revealable ladder is a strong anchor for the factor-string meaning of exponents and directly targets the 10³ = 30 confusion, though on its own it shows values rather than the shifting action.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.2: explain patterns in zeros and decimal-point placement for ×/÷ by powers of 10 and use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10.
learnerActions: Reveal each power from 10¹ to 10⁶ one at a time, writing its expanded factor string and ordinary value (e.g. 10⁴ = 10×10×10×10 = 10000).
For each, state the number of factors of ten and the number of zeros, and note that they match for these whole-number powers.
Contrast 10³ = 10×10×10 = 1000 with 10×3 = 30 aloud, so the exponent is not mistaken for a plain multiplier.
activities.intendedInsight: An exponent is a count of factors of ten, and for a power of ten written on its own the zero-count equals that factor count — while 10³ is emphatically not 10×3.

activities.title: Defend it against the 'add zeros' rule
feedback: If the learner cannot explain beyond the rule, ask them to say where each digit lands column by column.
Press for 'how many times bigger/smaller' to connect the exponent to the factor (100 for 10², 1000 for 10³).
activities.rationale: Requiring a spoken or written justification, not just an answer, discriminates understanding of the pattern from mimicry of a shortcut.
learnerActions: Face a prompt such as: 'A classmate says 3.4 × 10² = 3.400. Explain why that is wrong and give the correct answer.'
Justify using the digit shift: each ×10 moves the digits one column left, so 3.4 → 34 → 340.
Answer and explain 2.56 × 10³ (= 2560) and 2.56 ÷ 10³ (= 0.00256), saying how multiplication and division differ in shift direction.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the place-value shift exposes why 'add a zero' only looks right when the point sits at the end of a whole number, and why it fails for decimals; the zeros that do appear are placeholders for emptied columns.

activities.title: Predict-and-check consolidation
feedback: For 2.56 × 10³ the answer is 2560; 2.56000 just glues zeros on without shifting; 0.00256 divides instead of multiplies; 76.8 treats 10³ as 30.
Use any wrong choice as a cue to return to the place-value chart for that case.
activities.rationale: Short selected- and filled-response items can efficiently consolidate the pattern and surface the three named misconceptions as distractors; this checks that the pattern holds rather than demonstrating why it holds, so keep a task that requires a constructed explanation alongside it.
learnerActions: Complete items such as: fill in 10³ = ____; and choose the correct value of 2.56 × 10³ from options that include the add-zeros error 2.56000, the wrong-direction error 0.00256, and the exponent-as-multiplier error 76.8.
Put 10¹, 10², 10³, 10⁴, 10⁵ in order and match each to its zero count.
For each item, write one sentence saying why the chosen answer is right.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall that each power of ten corresponds to a fixed number of place-value shifts, with common error patterns ruled out explicitly.

constraints: Define an exponent as the number of factors of ten (10³ = 10×10×10), never as 'the number of zeros' — the zero-count of the power of ten is a consequence, and the 'add that many zeros' rule works only for whole-number products and breaks for decimals.

Distinguish appended zeros from placeholder zeros: multiplying a decimal does not append zeros after its decimal point to the original digits, but placeholder zeros may legitimately fill emptied whole-number columns (e.g. 340, 3400, 2560). Do not tell a learner 'no zeros appear' when the displayed product contains them.
Insist that the digits move and the decimal point stays fixed; avoid teaching 'move the decimal point' as the primary idea, though it can be mentioned as an equivalent description.
Include division by powers of ten alongside multiplication so the shift is seen as bidirectional.
The reference ladder is a static anchor: on its own it does not show the digit shift as an action, so pair it with the moving chart.
Selected-response consolidation checks the pattern but does not elicit the learner's own explanation; keep a task that requires constructing a justification.
Live recolouring/highlighting, digit sliding, a mobile exponent dial, zero tallies and a divide toggle are offered as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not as required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source lists one US standard citation as not verified (verified:false for 5.NBT.A.2); treat that citation's status as unconfirmed.

Clarified the lead activity's column-count wording so each total shift is tied to its exponent (10¹→one column, 10²→two columns, 10³→three columns), avoiding a reading where a single ×10 hop is labelled two columns.

Corrected the original 'the columns fill without any zeros being added' framing: 3.4 × 100 = 340 and 3.4 × 1000 = 3400 do contain placeholder zeros, and 34 → 340 appends a placeholder; the guidance distinguishes zeros appended after the decimal point (the 3.400 error) from placeholder zeros filling emptied columns.

The source's correct-answer phrasing 'the decimal point moves three places right' is retained only as an equivalent secondary description, subordinated to the 'digits move, point fixed' framing per the pedagogy's own best practice.

probeDeeper: Why does the answer get bigger, and by how many times exactly?
What does the little 3 in 10³ actually tell you to do?
Would 'add three zeros' work for 2.56 × 10³? Why or why not?
What is 2.56 ÷ 10³, and how is it different from multiplying?
assess.correctAnswer: 2,560. Multiplying by 10³ means ×1000, so every digit becomes worth a thousand times more and shifts three places to the left (equivalently the decimal point moves three places right, and a zero fills the empty ones place).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Add three zeros' rule — appends zeros to the written digits, giving 2.56000 for 2.56 × 10³.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that ×10 shifts every digit one place left (2.56→25.6→256→2560); the 'add a zero' shortcut only works for whole numbers because the point sits at the end.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Zeros are stuck onto the decimal without the point moving; answer keeps the decimal in place.

errorPatterns.pattern: Moves the point the wrong way — divides instead of multiplies, giving 0.00256.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor direction: multiplying makes it bigger, so digits move to larger places (left); rehearse on a place-value chart with the point fixed and digits sliding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer is smaller than the start; point moved left for a multiplication.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the exponent as a plain multiplier — reads 10³ as 30, so 2.56 × 10³ becomes 2.56 × 30 = 76.8.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Unpack 10³ = 10×10×10 = 1000; contrast with 10×3 = 30 so the exponent is seen as repeated multiplication.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child multiplies by 30 (or says 10³ = 30), confusing exponent with base×exponent.

responseLevels.gap: Appends zeros, moves the point the wrong way, or treats 10³ as 30.
responseLevels.full: Predicts the result via place-value shift, explains the exponent as repeated ×10, and handles decimals and both × and ÷ by powers of ten consistently.
responseLevels.partial: Gets whole-number cases right by rule but the pattern breaks with a decimal like 2.56, or cannot explain why the point moves.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Without calculating it out, what is 2.56 × 10³? Explain why the digits or the decimal point move the way they do.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the pattern explains it by place-value shift (×10 three times moves digits left) and correctly gets 2,560. A child running the 'add three zeros' rule writes 2.56000; one who thinks the exponent is a multiplier gets 76.8 (×30). The explanation, not just the answer, reveals whether the zero-pattern is understood or mimicked.
